selection_reason: 1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so every design choice is uncertain. Prior expectations favor multimodal fusion, multiprofile aggregation and stronger pretrained encoders, but none of these is confirmed on this dataset. 2. What this tests: config_041 combines the richest option on every axis: multimodal input, multiprofile with transformer aggregation, scGPT for RNA, ViT-L for images and weighted fusion. It sets a strong high-capacity reference point and shows whether the most expressive pipeline actually performs well here. 3. Why now: Only the best accuracy counts, so an early strong candidate is valuable. Later experiments can then ablate one factor at a time (RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation, fusion, single vs. multimodal) to check whether simpler variants match or beat it.

1) Evidence: only config_041 has been run (multimodal, multiprofile, scGPT, ViT-L, transformer, weighted), giving 0.422 accuracy and 0.405 F1. A single result tells us nothing yet about which design choices matter. 2) Test: config_004 keeps every setting identical except the RNA encoder, swapping scGPT for PCA with 2000 components. This isolates the effect of the RNA representation, which is likely one of the most influential choices. 3) Why now: a clean one-factor comparison against the only known result shows whether the foundation-model RNA embedding helps or a simple PCA baseline is competitive. That answer will guide the remaining 8 experiments, for example whether to try scVI next or to focus on aggregation and fusion.

1) Evidence: with everything else held fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, ViT-L, transformer, weighted), swapping scGPT for PCA raised accuracy from 0.422 to 0.542, and F1 rose with it. So the RNA encoder looks like a high-impact choice, but the third option, scVI, is still untested. 2) This run tests scVI in the same backbone, which completes the RNA-encoder comparison under controlled conditions. It will show whether PCA is truly the best encoder or whether scVI's learned latent space does even better. 3) Settling the most influential factor seen so far, before spending budget on fusion, aggregation or image-encoder variants, keeps later exploitation anchored to the right RNA encoder. The single-variable change also keeps the result easy to interpret.

1. Evidence: Three experiments varied only the RNA encoder, holding multiprofile, imagenet_vit_l, transformer aggregation and weighted fusion fixed. scvi_n200 was clearly best (0.591 acc, 0.573 F1), ahead of pca_n2000 (0.542) and scgpt (0.422). Every other design choice has been tested at only one value, so fusion, aggregation and image encoder remain uncertain. 2. Test: Keep the best setup but swap weighted fusion for concat fusion. This is a one-factor change, so any difference can be attributed to the fusion strategy. 3. Why now: It exploits the strongest region found so far while answering an open design question in a single run. The result will tell me which fusion to carry forward. Aggregation (config_034) and image encoder (config_025) can be checked with the remaining five experiments.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: Among multiprofile, transformer, weighted-fusion runs, scvi_n200 (0.591 acc, 0.573 F1) clearly beat pca_n2000 (0.542) and scgpt (0.422). For scvi_n200, weighted fusion also beat concat (0.591 vs 0.520), with F1 agreeing. So the best region is scvi_n200 with weighted fusion. The image encoder has never been varied, though: every run so far used imagenet_vit_l. 2. What this tests: config_025 keeps the best config_033 setup and changes only the image encoder to resnet50. That isolates whether the image backbone is a real lever for accuracy. 3. Why now: The image encoder is the largest untested design choice next to the current best. This one-variable test either finds a stronger backbone or confirms vit_l, so the remaining 4 experiments can focus on aggregation (avgpool) and the other factors.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_025 (scvi_n200 + resnet50 + transformer + weighted, 0.639 accuracy, 0.620 F1). The history supports scvi_n200 over pca_n2000 and scgpt, and weighted over concat fusion (0.591 vs 0.520). Switching from ViT-L to ResNet50 also gave a gain. Every run so far used transformer aggregation, so the aggregation choice is completely untested. 2. Test: config_016 changes only the aggregation, from transformer to avgpool, while keeping the best known setup fixed. This isolates whether a simpler pooling of profiles matches or beats transformer aggregation. 3. Why now: It is a low-risk exploit of the best configuration that also resolves the largest remaining uncertainty among the multiprofile multimodal choices. The answer will tell the last three experiments which aggregation to build on, for example for single-profile or unimodal comparisons.

1) Evidence: So far scVI beats PCA and scGPT, ResNet50 beats ViT-L, weighted fusion beats concat, and avgpool beat transformer aggregation. The best result is config_016 (scVI + ResNet50 + avgpool + weighted, 0.713 accuracy and 0.695 F1). That the simpler avgpool won suggests extra aggregation complexity may not help. However, every run so far has used multiprofile, so the profile setting is completely untested. 2) This run keeps the best scVI, ResNet50 and weighted-fusion components and switches to singleprofile, which has no aggregation. It tests whether multiprofile aggregation actually adds value or whether a simpler single-profile model does as well or better. 3) It is the most informative next run because it resolves a major untested design axis while still being a strong candidate to beat 0.713. That outcome will guide how to spend the last two experiments.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_016 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ResNet50, avgpool, weighted) at 0.713 accuracy, with F1 0.695. Several design choices each favour this setting in a single pairwise comparison: scVI beat PCA and scGPT, ResNet50 beat ViT-L, weighted fusion beat concat, avgpool beat transformer, and multiprofile beat singleprofile. These are one-off comparisons, so they are suggestive rather than conclusive. The main untested question is modality: no unimodal run exists, so we do not know whether the image branch actually adds value. Swapping the RNA encoder caused the largest swings (scGPT 0.42 vs scVI 0.59), which suggests the RNA signal dominates. 2. Test: config_045 runs RNA-only with scVI, multiprofile and avgpool, which is the best setup with the image branch removed. If it matches or beats 0.713, the image features are noise and RNA-only becomes a new best. If it falls short, we will know multimodal fusion adds value and can use the last experiment on a small tweak to config_016. 3. Why now: Further tweaks to config_016 are less promising. Concat, ViT-L and PCA each lost to the alternative used in config_016 in their one comparison. Testing modality reduces the largest remaining uncertainty and still has a realistic chance of producing a new best.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_016 (scvi_n200 + resnet50, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.713 accuracy and 0.695 F1. scvi_n200 has clearly beaten pca and scGPT. Weighted fusion beat concat, and avgpool beat transformer aggregation, which was a large gain of about 0.07. The ResNet50 vs ViT-L preference (0.639 vs 0.591) was measured only under transformer aggregation, so it may not hold under avgpool. 2) Test: This experiment keeps the best recipe (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted) and swaps the image encoder to imagenet_vit_l. It tests whether ViT-L features underperformed because of the transformer aggregator rather than the encoder itself. 3) Rationale: With two experiments left, a one-factor change to the top configuration offers the most plausible chance of beating 0.713. The other single-factor options have stronger negative prior evidence: concat fusion, pca or scGPT RNA encoders, and unimodal settings.

The best result so far is config_016 (scvi_n200 + resnet50 + avgpool + weighted, 0.713 acc / 0.695 F1). The evidence favors scvi_n200 over pca and scGPT, resnet50 over ViT-L, and avgpool over transformer when paired with resnet50. Fusion type has only been compared once, under the weaker ViT-L/transformer setup (weighted 0.591 vs concat 0.520), so it is still untested in the strongest backbone. This experiment keeps every winning component of config_016 and changes only the fusion to concat. Concat is not expected to be the favorite given the earlier result, but the other one-change neighbors look less likely to beat 0.713: pca and scGPT encoders were clearly weaker, and image-only lacks the RNA signal that drove the multimodal gain. As the final experiment, the best use is the closest untested change to the top configuration, with only fusion left uncertain.

1) There is no history yet, so every design choice is uncertain: modality, single vs. multi-profile, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation and fusion. 2) This run tests a strong-prior anchor: multimodal, multiprofile, the pretrained scGPT RNA encoder, the large ImageNet ViT-L image encoder, transformer aggregation and weighted fusion. If the full-featured setup does well, it sets a high baseline. Later runs can then remove one factor at a time (e.g., avgpool, concat, a different RNA encoder, single-profile, unimodal) to see which components matter. 3) Since only the best accuracy counts, starting from the configuration most likely to score well gives early exploitation value. It also gives a clear reference point for efficient one-factor ablations with the remaining 9 runs.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: We have one result, config_051 (multimodal, multiprofile, scGPT + ImageNet ViT-L, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion), at 0.635 accuracy and 0.618 F1. With a single data point we cannot yet tell which design choices drive performance. 2. What this tests: config_001 changes only the image encoder, from ViT-L to ResNet50, and keeps everything else fixed. That isolates the effect of the image backbone, which is likely a high-impact choice for the image modality. 3. Why it is the best next use of the budget: a one-factor change around the current best gives a clean answer we can interpret directly. If ViT-L clearly wins, we can fix it and spend the remaining budget on the RNA encoder, aggregation, fusion and profile setting. If ResNet50 wins, we redirect the search toward it early.

1) Evidence: with scGPT, transformer aggregation and weighted fusion held fixed, ImageNet ViT-L (0.635 acc, 0.618 F1) beat ResNet50 (0.619 acc, 0.610 F1). The gap is small, but it points to ViT-L as the better image encoder for now. The RNA encoder is still completely unexplored, and it is a major design choice with three options. 2) This experiment keeps the current best setup (multiprofile, ViT-L, transformer, weighted) and swaps only scGPT for scVI. That isolates how much the RNA representation matters relative to the image encoder. 3) Under a limited budget, it builds on the most promising setup while resolving a high-impact uncertainty. If scVI matches or beats scGPT, PCA and then the fusion and aggregation variants become the next things to check. If scGPT wins, later experiments can focus on fusion (concat) and aggregation (avgpool) around the scGPT + ViT-L setup.

1. Evidence: The RNA encoder has shown the largest effect so far. With vit_l, transformer aggregation and weighted fusion held fixed, scvi_n200 scored 0.678 accuracy versus 0.635 for scgpt. The vit_l image encoder also beat resnet50 under scgpt (0.635 vs 0.619). The third RNA encoder, pca_n2000, has not been tested in any setting. 2. Test: config_043 swaps in pca_n2000 while keeping the best-known setup (vit_l, transformer, weighted). This isolates the RNA encoder choice and completes the three-way comparison. 3. Why now: The RNA encoder is the design choice with the largest observed impact, and one of its options is entirely unexplored. Settling it first means the remaining six experiments can tune fusion (concat vs weighted) and aggregation (avgpool vs transformer) on the strongest RNA encoder. It also has a realistic chance of beating the current best.

1) Evidence: all four runs held fusion=weighted and aggregation=transformer fixed. Only the encoders varied. The RNA encoder had the largest effect: pca_n2000 (0.721 acc / 0.681 F1) > scvi_n200 (0.678) > scgpt (0.635). For image encoders, ViT-L beat ResNet50 with scgpt (0.635 vs 0.619). Fusion and aggregation have not been tested at all, so their effects are the biggest open uncertainty. 2) Test: config_040 keeps the best configuration (pca_n2000 + imagenet_vit_l + multiprofile transformer) and changes only fusion, from weighted to concat. This cleanly isolates the fusion effect on the strongest backbone. 3) Why now: it exploits the best region while resolving an untested design axis with a one-factor change. If concat helps, later runs can build on it. If it does not, weighted is confirmed and the remaining budget can go to the aggregation choice (config_045) and an RNA-only check (config_019).

1) Evidence: config_043 (pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) leads at 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. Weighted fusion clearly beat concat (0.527), and pca_n2000 beat scvi_n200 and scgpt with the ViT-L image encoder. Aggregation has not been varied yet: every run so far used the transformer. 2) This run keeps the best configuration fixed and swaps only the aggregation to avgpool. That isolates whether the transformer aggregator is actually helping or whether a simpler pooling does as well or better. 3) Aggregation is the main untested design choice inside the leading multiprofile setup. A one-factor change from the best run either may raise the best score directly or confirms the transformer, so the remaining budget can go to profile setting or single-modality checks.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: Among multiprofile multimodal runs, the best setup is pca_n2000 RNA + imagenet_vit_l + transformer aggregation + weighted fusion (0.721 acc, 0.681 F1). Switching to concat fusion (0.527) or avgpool aggregation (0.332) hurt it badly. RNA encoder choice also mattered (pca > scvi > scgpt). Image encoder choice looked minor (ViT-L 0.635 vs ResNet50 0.619 with scGPT). The profile setting is the one major design axis not yet tested: every run so far has been multiprofile. 2. What this tests: config_008 keeps the best encoders and weighted fusion but uses singleprofile input. This shows whether multiprofile aggregation is needed or whether a simpler single-profile model can match or beat 0.721, given that the aggregation choice clearly matters a lot. 3. Why now: Re-checking the image encoder (config_027) is likely to give only a small change, and fusion and aggregation already have clear answers. Testing profile setting resolves the largest remaining uncertainty with the strongest known components. That leaves 3 experiments to refine whichever profile setting wins, for example with a ResNet50 or RNA-only check.

1. Evidence: the best result so far is config_043 (PCA-2000 RNA, ViT-L image, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) at 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. Ablations around it show that transformer aggregation, weighted fusion and multiprofile input are all strongly preferred. RNA encoder choice also matters a lot: PCA beat scVI, which beat scGPT. The image encoder is the least resolved choice. Its only comparison is with scGPT, where ViT-L beat ResNet50 by 0.635 vs 0.619, a gap too small to be conclusive. 2. Test: config_027 swaps ViT-L for ResNet50 and keeps every other winning setting. This isolates the image encoder within the best-performing context and checks whether ResNet50 pairs better with PCA features. 3. Value: the other design axes are already well settled, so this is the main remaining choice that could plausibly beat 0.721. It also tells us how to use the final experiment, for example whether an RNA-only PCA transformer baseline is worth checking.

Evidence: config_043 (pca_n2000 + imagenet_vit_l, multiprofile transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) leads at 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. Each of its choices beat the alternatives tested: pca_n2000 beat scvi_n200 and scgpt, imagenet_vit_l beat resnet50, transformer beat avgpool, weighted beat concat, and multiprofile beat singleprofile. Every remaining multimodal option changes at least one of these winning choices, so none is likely to beat it. The biggest open question is whether the image branch helps at all. RNA encoder choice causes the largest swings (0.635 to 0.721), so the RNA representation may carry most of the signal. The image encoder effect (0.639 vs 0.721 with pca) suggests images contribute, but no unimodal baseline has been run. What this tests: config_019 keeps the strongest RNA encoder and the best aggregation but drops the image branch. If it beats 0.721, image fusion was adding noise and we have a new best. If not, we confirm that multimodal fusion helps. Why now: it is the remaining configuration with the most credible chance of exceeding config_043 while also settling a major design question, leaving one experiment for a final follow-up.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_043 (pca_n2000 + imagenet_vit_l, multiprofile, transformer, weighted) at 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. Every single-factor change from it lowered accuracy. Concat fell to 0.527, avgpool to 0.331, singleprofile to 0.525, resnet50 to 0.639, and scvi or scgpt RNA encoders to 0.678 and 0.635. RNA-only with transformer reached 0.579. ViT-L was clearly the stronger image encoder. The image-only contribution is still unknown. 2) Test: config_005 is image-only with ViT-L, multiprofile and transformer aggregation. It measures how much of the multimodal gain comes from the image branch, and whether RNA features add noise. 3) Why this one: with one experiment left, the remaining multimodal options are each one step away from config_043 in directions that already hurt. The closest untested one, config_033 (scvi + resnet50), is likely to land around 0.62–0.64, below the current best. Image-only ViT-L keeps the two settings that worked best (multiprofile and transformer) and drops RNA. It is the most plausible remaining way to beat 0.72, though that is not likely, and if it falls short it still clarifies which modality drives performance.

1) No experiments have been run yet, so there is no evidence about which modalities, encoders, aggregation or fusion methods work best. Priors suggest that multimodal, multi-profile models with strong pretrained encoders and learned aggregation are likely to perform best. 2) config_041 tests a strong-prior anchor: multimodal, multiprofile, scVI RNA embeddings, ImageNet ViT-L image features, transformer aggregation and concat fusion. Its result gives a high baseline, and later experiments can each change one factor (encoder, aggregation, fusion, profile setting) to see what matters. 3) With only 10 experiments and only the best accuracy counting, starting from a likely high performer secures a good result early. It also works as a reference point for targeted ablations and for exploring alternatives such as image-only or single-profile models.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: We have only one result so far. config_041 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ViT-L, transformer, concat) reached 0.332 accuracy and 0.315 F1. That gives a baseline but says nothing about which component drives performance. 2. What this tests: config_024 keeps every setting the same except the RNA encoder, which changes from scvi_n200 to the pretrained scGPT foundation model. This cleanly isolates the effect of RNA representation. The RNA encoder has three options and is likely one of the biggest sources of variation in multimodal cellular profiling. 3. Why it is the best next step: a one-factor change from the current best is easy to interpret. It also explores a potentially stronger encoder while staying in a configuration family that already works reasonably well. Whichever encoder wins tells us what to carry into later tests of aggregation, fusion, image encoder and profile setting.

1) Evidence: the only two runs differ just in RNA encoder. scGPT (0.706 acc, 0.667 F1) far outperformed scVI (0.332 acc). This is strong evidence that the RNA encoder is the dominant factor and that scGPT is the better choice. 2) This run keeps the best setup (scGPT, ImageNet ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer aggregation) and changes only the fusion from concat to weighted. That isolates whether a weighted fusion can make better use of the strong scGPT signal relative to the image features. 3) Changing one factor at a time on the current best is the best use of the budget now. It could directly improve the top accuracy, and the result stays easy to interpret. The remaining runs can then test image encoder, aggregation, or an RNA-only ablation around whichever fusion wins.

1) Evidence: The RNA encoder has been the largest driver so far. With ViT-L, transformer aggregation and concat fusion held fixed, scGPT scored 0.706 accuracy and scVI scored 0.332. Concat also beat weighted fusion for scGPT (0.706 vs 0.530 accuracy, with F1 following the same pattern). The third RNA option, PCA (2000 components), has not been tested. 2) Test: config_007 keeps the best setup (multimodal, multiprofile, ViT-L, transformer, concat) and swaps scGPT for PCA. This isolates the effect of the PCA encoder. 3) Rationale: Because the RNA encoder changed accuracy so much, an untested encoder is the most likely place to find a large gain or to confirm scGPT as the anchor. PCA is a strong baseline in many single-cell benchmarks, so it could match or beat scGPT. Settling this now lets later experiments on aggregation (avgpool) and image encoder (ResNet50) build on the best RNA encoder.

1) Evidence: the RNA encoder is the dominant factor so far. scGPT reached 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1, far above scVI (0.332) and PCA (0.224) in otherwise identical setups. Concat fusion also beat weighted fusion for scGPT (0.706 vs 0.530). Aggregation is completely untested, since every run used the transformer. 2) This run keeps the best setup (scGPT, ImageNet ViT-L, concat) and changes only aggregation from transformer to avgpool. That isolates whether simpler pooling across profiles matches or beats the transformer. 3) It exploits the strong scGPT plus concat direction while answering a major open design question with a single change. The result will tell me whether later experiments, such as swapping the image encoder to ResNet50, should use transformer or avgpool aggregation.

Evidence: the best result so far is config_024 (scGPT + ViT-L + transformer + concat, acc 0.706, F1 0.667). Single-factor comparisons against it all point the same way. scGPT clearly beats scVI (0.33) and PCA (0.22). Transformer aggregation beats avgpool (0.23). Concat fusion beats weighted (0.53). The F1 scores agree in each case. The image encoder is the one design choice in the multimodal multiprofile setting that has not been varied: every run so far used ViT-L. Test: config_003 keeps the winning scGPT/transformer/concat setup and swaps the image encoder to ResNet50. This isolates the effect of the image backbone. Why now: it is the remaining untested axis, and it is a direct one-change variant of the best configuration, so it could beat 0.706. If ResNet50 does worse, ViT-L is confirmed and the last 3 experiments can go to other checks, such as RNA-only scGPT with transformer (config_046) to see how much the images add.

Evidence: the best result so far is scGPT + ViT-L + transformer aggregation + concat fusion (0.706 accuracy, 0.667 F1). Every single-factor change from it made things worse. Weaker RNA encoders scored 0.22–0.33, avgpool scored 0.23, weighted fusion scored 0.53 and ResNet50 scored 0.52. So scGPT and transformer aggregation look essential. Still untested is whether the image branch actually adds value or partly adds noise. This experiment keeps the strongest parts (scGPT, multiprofile, transformer) and drops the image branch, which isolates how much the RNA side contributes. If RNA-only matches or beats 0.706, the remaining budget should go to RNA-centric variants. If it drops clearly, the multimodal ViT-L setup is confirmed, and the last experiments can target the singleprofile question with confidence. It is the untested candidate most likely to rival the current best while also resolving a key design question.

1. Evidence: the best result so far is config_024 (scGPT + ViT-L + transformer + concat, multiprofile) at 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1. Single changes from it all hurt. Weighted fusion dropped to 0.530, avgpool to 0.227, ResNet50 to 0.518, and RNA-only to 0.591. scVI and PCA encoders were also much weaker. So scGPT, ViT-L and concat fusion look well supported. The one major choice never tested is the profile setting: every run so far used multiprofile. 2. Test: config_043 keeps the best encoders and concat fusion but switches to singleprofile, which removes the aggregation step. This shows whether multiprofile with transformer aggregation is truly needed, or whether a simpler single-profile model can match or beat 0.706. 3. Why now: with two experiments left, this is the largest remaining uncertainty that could still raise the best score. Other untested configs mostly combine options that already did poorly. If singleprofile does well, the last experiment can refine it; if not, config_024 stands as the confirmed best.

1. Evidence: config_024 (multimodal, multiprofile, scGPT, ViT-L, transformer, concat) is the clear best at 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1. Every one-factor change from it scored lower: weighted fusion 0.530, ResNet50 0.518, avgpool 0.227, singleprofile 0.512, scVI 0.332, PCA 0.224, and dropping the image branch (RNA-only) 0.591. The one neighbouring change not yet tested is removing the RNA branch, which is config_048 (image-only, ViT-L, transformer, multiprofile). 2. Question: this measures how much ViT-L image features carry on their own under the best aggregation setup. That tells us whether the 0.706 comes from complementary fusion or mostly from one modality. The weak multimodal runs with poor RNA encoders (0.22–0.33) suggest image-only will probably land below 0.706, but this has never been measured directly. 3. Why this is the best use: the remaining two-factor variants combine changes that each hurt individually, such as weighted fusion with ResNet50 or with avgpool, so they are unlikely to beat 0.706. config_048 completes the single-factor check around the best configuration with one experiment and leaves the final experiment for a last attempt informed by the result.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_024 (scGPT + ViT-L + transformer + concat, 0.706 accuracy, 0.667 F1). The two choices that matter most are the scGPT RNA encoder and transformer aggregation. Replacing scGPT with scVI or PCA dropped accuracy to 0.33 and 0.22. Replacing the transformer with avgpool dropped it to 0.23. The single-profile setting and the unimodal models also scored clearly lower. Fusion and image encoder are smaller, secondary effects. Weighted fusion hurt with ViT-L (0.53), and ResNet50 with concat reached 0.52, but these are single runs and their combination is untested. 2. What this tests: config_029 is the only untested configuration that keeps both key choices (scGPT and multi-profile transformer aggregation) in the multimodal setting. It checks whether weighted fusion works better with ResNet50 features than it did with ViT-L. 3. Why it is the best final pick: With no experiments left, only the best accuracy found counts. Every other remaining option drops scGPT or the transformer, which has consistently cut performance sharply. config_029 has the highest prior chance among the remaining options of matching or beating 0.706, though it is still more likely to fall short.

1) No experiments have been run yet, so there is no evidence on any design choice. The usual prior is that multimodal, multi-profile models with strong pretrained encoders and learned aggregation do best on cellular profiling tasks, but this has not been tested here. 2) config_005 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200 RNA encoder, ImageNet ViT-L image encoder, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) is a strong, central candidate. It gives an early high-performing anchor and a reference point for one-factor-at-a-time comparisons in later experiments: weighted vs. concat fusion (config_003), avgpool vs. transformer aggregation (config_050), the RNA encoder (config_030, config_042), the image encoder (config_051), and the unimodal ablations (config_034, config_048). 3) With only 10 experiments and the best accuracy being what counts, starting from a likely-strong configuration that has many single-change neighbors serves both goals. It gives a good chance of an early high score and makes each later experiment informative about one design choice.

1) Evidence: only one result exists, config_005 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200 + ViT-L, transformer aggregation, concat), with 0.536 accuracy and 0.516 F1. One point says nothing about which design choices drive performance. 2) Test: config_013 keeps the same RNA encoder, image encoder and concat fusion but switches to single-profile, so aggregation is removed. This isolates whether multi-profile aggregation adds value over single-profile inputs. 3) Why now: profile setting decides whether the aggregation dimension (transformer vs avgpool) matters at all, and it splits a large part of the remaining search space. A clean one-factor comparison against the current best tells us where to spend the remaining 8 experiments. The other options would be finer-grained tweaks, such as fusion type or encoder swaps, which matter less until this is settled.

Evidence: the multiprofile setup with transformer aggregation (config_005, acc 0.536, F1 0.516) beat the matched singleprofile setup (config_013, acc 0.514, F1 0.498). Both accuracy and F1 point the same way, but with only two runs this is modest support for multiprofile aggregation. The RNA encoder is a major untested design choice. This experiment keeps everything from the current best (multiprofile, ViT-L image encoder, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) and swaps only the RNA encoder from scVI to scGPT. That isolates whether a foundation-model RNA embedding adds signal. With 7 experiments left, a one-factor change from the current best gives a clean comparison on a high-impact axis. Fusion, aggregation and image-encoder variants can then be built on whichever RNA encoder wins.

1) Evidence: switching the RNA encoder from scvi_n200 to scgpt, with everything else fixed (multiprofile, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, concat), raised validation accuracy from 0.536 to 0.678, and F1 rose with it. That makes scgpt with transformer aggregation the clear lead. Multiprofile beat singleprofile in the scvi comparison (0.536 vs 0.514), though that gap is small. Fusion type is still completely untested. 2) This experiment keeps the best configuration unchanged except for swapping concat fusion for weighted fusion, so any difference can be attributed to the fusion choice. 3) It exploits the strongest direction found so far while settling an untested design choice that could add further gains. Aggregation, image encoder and the unimodal baselines can be tested in the remaining budget.

1. Evidence: The RNA encoder has had the largest effect so far. Swapping scvi_n200 for scgpt raised accuracy from 0.536 to 0.678 with transformer aggregation and concat fusion. Weighted fusion then gave a small further gain to 0.688 (F1 0.659). The third RNA encoder, pca_n2000, is still untested, and simple PCA features are often competitive with foundation-model embeddings. 2. Test: This keeps the best-known setup (multiprofile, imagenet_vit_l, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) and changes only the RNA encoder to pca_n2000. It shows whether scgpt is truly the best choice on the factor with the highest observed sensitivity. 3. Why now: Leaving a high-impact factor partly unexplored carries more risk than checking lower-impact choices first.
